problems: stop 1 card 2, answer 1: copies a Prep line word for word

explanations.explanation: Paul says plainly, “It is for freedom that Christ has set us free,” and he tells them to stand firm (Gal 5:1). He means don’t let anyone haul you back under a yoke of slavery after Christ has freed you.

explanations.answer: Work hard to earn their freedom
explanations.explanation: That’s not Paul’s point. He insists freedom comes because Christ set them free, not by earning it (Gal 5:1–2). Trying to earn it by returning to the law would undo the freedom Christ bought.
Paul doesn’t say be silent. He warns them to stand firm in the freedom Christ gave them, not to let it be taken away (Gal 5:1). The focus is on holding to what they’ve received, not hiding it.
True — Paul warns them not to be burdened again by a yoke of slavery (Gal 5:1). The image is clear: don’t let legalism pull you back under obligations that Christ freed you from.
False is wrong here. Paul explicitly says don’t be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery, so he is warning them about being weighed down again (Gal 5:1).
Paul signs his name and says bluntly: if they get circumcised, Christ will be of no value to them (Gal 5:2). He means relying on that rite as a means of salvation nullifies what Christ accomplished.
That’s the opposite of what Paul says. He warns that being circumcised with the aim of justification would make Christ of no value to them (Gal 5:2).
Paul doesn’t say it’s equal. He warns that if they submit to circumcision as a requirement, they lose the value of Christ for them — it amounts to rejecting what He did (Gal 5:2).
That answer is incorrect. Paul says a man who gets circumcised is obligated to obey the whole law, not just that one command (Gal 5:3). Circumcision would bring the full burden of the law on him.
Correct — Paul actually says the opposite of the statement. He warns that if someone is circumcised they become obligated to keep the whole law (Gal 5:3).

explanations.answer: They have been severed from Christ
explanations.explanation: That’s what Paul says: those trying to be justified by the law have been severed from Christ and have fallen from grace (Gal 5:4). Relying on the law for justification breaks the union with Christ.

explanations.answer: They have drawn closer to Christ
explanations.explanation: Paul says the opposite. Trying to be justified by the law cuts you off from Christ rather than bringing you closer (Gal 5:4).
Paul doesn’t promise extra grace for law-keeping. He warns that seeking justification by the law means falling away from grace (Gal 5:4). Grace and law are not additive here.
Paul says it’s by faith that we eagerly wait through the Spirit for the hope of righteousness (Gal 5:5). Faith is the posture of trusting God’s promise rather than relying on law-works.
That’s not what Paul says. He contrasts faith with relying on the law — he says they wait by faith through the Spirit for righteousness, not by the law (Gal 5:5–6).
Paul doesn’t put eager waiting under human effort. He says it’s by faith, through the Spirit, that they await the hope of righteousness (Gal 5:5).
Paul says exactly that: in Christ neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts — what matters is faith expressing itself through love (Gal 5:6). The proof of true faith is love in action.
Paul rejects that standard as the measure here. He says circumcision and its opposite have no value in Christ; what counts is faith working through love (Gal 5:6).

explanations.answer: Coming from the right family line
explanations.explanation: Lineage isn’t Paul’s point. He says external status like circumcision doesn’t matter in Christ; faith working by love is what matters (Gal 5:6).
That’s wrong. Paul says the persuasion obstructing them does not come from the One who calls them — in other words, it’s not from God (Gal 5:8).
Correct — Paul warns that the persuasion slowing them down does not come from the One who calls them (Gal 5:8). It’s a misleading influence, not God’s voice.
Paul uses the leaven picture: a little leaven works through the whole batch of dough (Gal 5:9). A small corrupting influence can spread and spoil the whole community.
Paul’s image is broader — he says a little leaven works through the whole batch, not merely the surface (Gal 5:9). The point is widespread effect.
Paul doesn’t limit the effect that narrowly. He warns that a little leaven will work through the whole batch of dough (Gal 5:9).
Paul says he is confident the one troubling them will bear the judgment, whatever his identity (Gal 5:10). Paul trusts the Lord to deal with false teachers.

explanations.answer: He will be let off free
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn’t expect mercy for the troublemaker; he says that person will bear the judgment (Gal 5:10). The confident note is that God will set things right.

explanations.answer: He will be put in charge
explanations.explanation: Paul never suggests the agitator will be promoted. He says the one troubling them will bear judgment, not leadership (Gal 5:10).
That would be incorrect. Paul asks rhetorically — if he were preaching circumcision, why would he be persecuted? He’s denying that he preaches circumcision (Gal 5:11).
Correct — Paul is denying that he preaches circumcision. He argues that if he preached it, the offense of the cross would be gone; since he’s persecuted, he’s not promoting circumcision (Gal 5:11).

That’s right — Paul reminds them they were called to freedom and warns not to use that freedom as an opportunity for the flesh (Gal 5:13). Freedom is for serving one another in love, not selfish indulgence.
That’s not what Paul says. He explicitly warns them not to use freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but to serve one another in love (Gal 5:13).
Paul says the entire law is fulfilled in the single decree, “Love your neighbor as yourself” (Gal 5:14). Love summarizes the law’s intent and guides Christian behavior.
Paul doesn’t single out Sabbath-keeping here. He says the law is fulfilled in loving your neighbor as yourself (Gal 5:14). The emphasis is on love, not ritual observance.
That command is part of the law, but Paul points to the general rule — love your neighbor as yourself — as fulfilling the whole law (Gal 5:14).
Paul warns that if they keep biting and devouring one another, they will be consumed by one another (Gal 5:15). Hostility among them will destroy the community.
That’s not the word Paul uses here. He warns they will be consumed by one another, a stronger image of mutual destruction (Gal 5:15).
Paul’s language is harsher — he says they will be consumed by one another, not merely shamed (Gal 5:15). The point is how destructive internal strife can be.
